extracted.intended_audience: scientists, philosophers of science, and students of scientific method
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and methodological rules for forming, testing, and accepting scientific hypotheses; covers the roles of induction, deduction, verification, and the limits on legitimate hypothesis-making with examples (Newton, vortices, ether).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of hypothesis
rubrics_metrics.description: An hypothesis is any supposition which we make (either without actual evidence, or on evidence avowedly insufficient) in order to endeavor to deduce from it conclusions in accordance with facts which are known to be real.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hypotheses are provisional suppositions used to enable deductive application to phenomena; they may concern causes, modes of production, or laws of correspondence between varying facts. Accept that hypotheses are tentative starting points for deduction and further inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-part process for deductive discovery (induction, ratiocination, verification)
rubrics_metrics.description: To discover the cause of any phenomenon by the Deductive Method, the process must consist of three parts: induction (to ascertain the laws of the causes), ratiocination (to compute from those laws how the causes will operate in the particular case), and verification (by comparing the calculated effect with the actual phenomenon). No one of these three parts can be dispensed with.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a proposed deductive proof of causation, check that all three steps are present or that equivalent prior deductions supply the induction. Example: Newton's identification of central force used all three steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothetical Method suppresses induction and requires verification to function as induction
rubrics_metrics.description: The Hypothetical Method suppresses the first step (induction) and contents itself with ratiocination and verification; the law which is reasoned from being assumed instead of proved. This is legitimate only if the final verification amounts to a complete induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether verification rules out all alternative laws — i.e., ensure no false law could produce the same observed consequences. If verification cannot fulfill the role of induction, the hypothetical conclusion remains weak.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement that verification rule out alternative laws (unique consequence condition)
rubrics_metrics.description: The hypothetical process is legitimate if the case be such that a false law cannot lead to a true result; provided no law, except the very one which we have assumed, can lead deductively to the same conclusions which that leads to.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for demonstrations (deductive or experimental) that the assumed law is the only antecedent that could produce the observed effects (as Newton did by showing alternatives would not give Kepler's laws). If uniqueness is not shown, do not accept the hypothesis as proved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer hypotheses about laws of an already ascertained cause
rubrics_metrics.description: It is a condition of the most genuinely scientific hypothesis that it be of such a nature as to be either proved or disproved by comparison with observed facts; this condition is fulfilled when the effect is already known to depend on the very cause supposed, and the hypothesis relates only to the precise mode of dependence (the law).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hypotheses that refine the law of a known cause (e.g., determining mathematical relation) are stronger because negative instances can be obtained and uniqueness demonstrated more readily.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vera causa requirement: proposed cause must be susceptible of independent proof
rubrics_metrics.description: The cause, though not known previously, should be capable of being known thereafter; its existence should be capable of being detected, and its connection with the effect ascribed to it should be susceptible of being proved by independent evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a hypothesis posits a new cause, require that the hypothesized agent be empirically detectable or that the hypothesis suggests independent observations/experiments that could establish its reality. Example anti-pattern: vortices that could not be directly shown to exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypotheses are legitimate investigative tools but remain conjectural until independently verified
rubrics_metrics.description: Hypotheses are necessary steps in the progress to something more certain; the hypothesis, by suggesting observations and experiments, puts us on the road to independent evidence, and till it be attained, the hypothesis ought only to count for a more or less plausible conjecture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat hypotheses as heuristic devices that guide experiment and observation; do not elevate them to truth until verification by independent evidence is achieved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plausibility by analogy with known laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Either the phenomenon assigned as the cause is real but the law merely supposed; or the cause is fictitious but is supposed to produce its effects according to laws similar to those of some known class of phenomena. Hypotheses that ally themselves by analogy with known laws have more plausibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give greater initial credence to hypotheses that map onto familiar mechanisms or laws; arbitrary inventions of unknown agents with fictitious laws lack plausibility and are weaker starting points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictive success alone is insufficient proof
rubrics_metrics.description: It is strange that any considerable stress should be laid upon the coincidence of predictions and their fulfillment; though such predictions are well calculated to impress the uninformed, they do not prove the reality of the underlying mechanism, because different hypotheses can lead to identical predictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a hypothesis yields successful predictions, evaluate whether alternative hypotheses could equally account for those predictions. Use additional independent tests that discriminate between competing hypotheses rather than relying solely on predictive coincidences (example: undulatory theory predictions do not by themselves prove an ether).

rubrics_metrics.name: Start with the simplest supposition and iterate (methods of approximation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The simplest supposition which accords with the more obvious facts is the best to begin with; this rude hypothesis is then rudely corrected, and the operation repeated... we arrive, by means of hypotheses, at conclusions not hypothetical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor simpler hypotheses that explain obvious facts, then refine by successive approximations comparing deductive consequences to observations. This is analogous to mathematicians' Methods of Approximation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypotheses must allow obtaining both affirmative and negative instances required by Method of Difference
rubrics_metrics.description: In order that a hypothetical assumption become proved, we must be able to obtain both the instances which the Method of Difference requires: the affirmative instance (A B C → a b c) and the negative instance (B C → b c), showing that no antecedent except the assumed one in conjunction with the background produces the effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the hypothesis furnishes or allows construction of the negative instance that rules out alternatives. If the negative instance cannot be obtained (e.g., cause wholly novel and not isolatable), the hypothesis cannot be elevated to induction by this method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical/forensic inference criterion: infer past causes only when no other known cause could generate the effects
rubrics_metrics.description: When we find masses or effects similar to those produced by known agents, we may justly conclude that such has been their origin; it is enough for most purposes, if no other known cause could have generated the effects shown to have been produced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In geological or judicial inferences about past events, accept hypotheses that attribute past effects to known agents when alternative known causes are implausible; still avoid overreaching beyond what circumstantial evidence warrants.
